html:
The Pure Food and Drug Act was a United States law signed by President Theodore Roosevelt on 30 June 1906. It was the first federal law to ban food and medicine that was falsely labelled or contaminated with harmful additives.

Before it, there were no national rules on what could go into food or patent medicines, and many products were adulterated or laced with dangerous drugs. The chemist Harvey Washington Wiley had pushed for reform for years, partly through his "Poison Squad" tests. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, which described filthy meatpacking plants in Chicago, stirred public anger just as Congress was debating, and a separate Meat Inspection Act passed the same day.

The law forbade the sale of misbranded or adulterated food and drugs across state lines and required honest labels. Its enforcement office later grew into the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It was an early success of the Progressive Era, when reformers used the federal government to regulate business.
